@AMD  and @Meta @Muse  are positioned to jointly win the consumer, small business, and enterprise agentic AI race. Meta’s Muse agent now powered by the new Muse Wonder frontier models gives every user a dedicated Secure VM (an isolated cloud computer with browser, terminal, files, and persistent memory). These VMs run on high density AMD EPYC server CPUs (Turin and next gen Venice class chips), while GPUs handle model inference. OpenAI’s Dots follow a similar pattern and also run on EPYC. This architecture is the key, where agents don’t just generate tokens, they orchestrate multi step workflows, use tools, recover from errors, and keep working for hours or days. That persistent runtime layer is CPU bound, and AMD’s core dense EPYC processors are purpose built for packing large numbers of agent sandboxes efficiently.

Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are Meta’s first true frontier models from Superintelligence Labs. They upgrade the earlier Muse Spark family with stronger Active Memory (retaining and retrieving user context across days, weeks, and months) and Active Focus (sustained effort, alternative approaches, and error recovery on hard tasks). Meta’s benchmarks show particular strength in personal and professional agentic work, legal document tasks (Harvey LAB), finance analysis, long horizon coding (SWE-Marathon), business automation, and an internal Personal Superintelligence Index; areas that matter far more for everyday users and small teams than pure leaderboard scores. Wonder will roll into the Muse app (subscribers first) and is already available via the Meta Model API and Muse Code.

Pricing and access reflect the frontier positioning: Muse Wonder on the Meta Model API is roughly $4 / $20 per million input/output tokens (comparable to high end Claude/GPT pricing); Wonder Full is reserved for Muse Code subscribers (higher tier plans in the ~$50–$200 range). Context is 1M tokens; modalities include text, image, video, and audio input.

While a basic single agent Muse session can operate efficiently inside one user’s Secure VM on roughly 2 vCPUs, delegating work to multiple sub-agents multiplies the compute footprint. Muse Code documentation shows concurrent child agent limits that are explicitly CPU derived (defaults around 8 simultaneous agents including the root, configurable higher, with queuing beyond that and support for up to 1,000 child tasks over a workflow’s lifetime). Parallel tool calls, isolated worktrees, independent sub tasks, and long running concurrent execution all increase CPU core demand, memory bandwidth, and scheduling overhead inside the sandbox. At consumer and small business scale this raises the average cores per active user; at enterprise or high volume multi agent deployments it drives the need for denser high core count EPYC flagship hosts and larger rack scale systems (such as AMD’s Helion designs with up to 32,768 cores in a CPU only configuration). The result is a steeper curve of CPU infrastructure growth more sandboxes, more cores per rack, and higher overall utilization to keep multi agent workflows responsive and non-blocking rather than serialized or throttled. This further amplifies the long term demand signal for AMD to innovate higher density server CPUs as Meta’s Muse ecosystem (and similar agent platforms) expands to 100-1,000 agents capabilities in the coming quarters/years!

1. Massive Fuel for AMD CPU Growth (Next 3–5 Years)

This is significant. Pure chatbot inference is heavily GPU bound. Persistent personal/professional agents change the mix: each user needs a dedicated (or densely packed) virtual machine with CPU cores, memory, and storage for long running workflows, browser use, code execution, file management, and background tasks, while GPUs handle the model inference.

Muse (and OpenAI Dots) already run on AMD EPYC high core density server CPUs. Reports from the initial Muse launch showed AMD EPYC Turin hosts, with agents themselves reporting the hardware. High core counts (128+ class) allow packing many user VMs per physical server. As Muse scales already millions of downloads shortly after launch, with daily actives in the millions and Zuckerberg’s stated ambition toward broader personal superintelligence, the CPU demand multiplies potentially 50-100x. Analysts have highlighted agents as a CPU demand driver; AMD’s data center CPU business has been strong, and Meta is a major existing EPYC customer.

Projections around the agent wave make this a multi year tailwind. The 3–5 year horizon aligns with continued growth in personal agents, more complex multi agent workflows, higher utilization of the VMs, and broader geographic/rollout expansion. AMD GPUs remain critical for training and inference, but the agent runtime layer is a distinct, large CPU opportunity that Wonder’s capabilities will help expand by making the agents more useful and sticky.

2. Upgraded Version of Regular Muse / Muse Spark + Continued VM Usage

Muse Spark was the deliberate first rung: smaller, faster, capable enough for early agent work but not frontier. Wonder is the larger, more advanced class that “brings us to the frontier,” with better post training gains on stronger base models, stronger out of distribution generalization, and the Active Memory / Active Focus features. It will continue powering (and upgrading) the same Muse agent architecture that launched not long ago.

The VM model stays central. Meta’s security write-ups describe each user’s Muse Secure VM as an isolated Linux environment with enough CPU, memory, and storage for real work (code compilation, custom tools, concurrent sub agents, persistent files and memory). Typical reported specs have been ~2 vCPUs and ~8 GB RAM per user on high-density AMD EPYC Turin hosts (9D25-class chips), with inference on separate GPU infrastructure. The design prioritizes isolation, credential protection via Sentinel, and the ability for the agent to act as if it has “a computer under the desk.” Wonder’s improvements in persistence, memory, focus, coding, and tool use make that VM more capable rather than replacing it.⁠

3. Small Businesses and Personal Agentic Usefulness

This is where the combination of frontier agent models + dedicated persistent VM shines for non enterprise users:

Personal use:

~Navigate multi step tasks that unfold over time (insurance claims, understanding a lease or medical information, personal financial analysis, calendar/message coordination, shopping or booking with confirmation gates).
~The agent remembers relevant details across sessions and keeps working toward the goal (with check-ins) on its own cloud computer, even when the user’s device is off.
~Lower barrier than pure professional coding agents because of the consumer facing Muse app, free tier with paid upgrades, and deep integration points.

Small businesses:

~Frontier coding for building or iterating apps, games, internal tools, or websites (strong SWE Marathon / long project results help here).
~Professional agent work in law (document drafting/review from source materials), finance (analysis, workflows), health-related queries, and business automation.
~A solo founder or small team can offload sustained, multi-step work (research + drafting + tool use + verification) to an agent that maintains context and operates inside a dedicated environment, without standing up their own infrastructure or large staff.
~Muse Code provides a developer facing path with the same models for heavier software workflows.

Conclusion:

For @finkd  , the stakes of the agentic superintelligence race are existential to Meta’s long term vision. As he wrote in his letter on personal superintelligence: “I am extremely optimistic that superintelligence will help humanity accelerate our pace of progress. But perhaps even more important is that superintelligence has the potential to begin a new era of personal empowerment where people will have greater agency to improve the world in the directions they choose.” He has repeatedly framed Meta’s goal as bringing “personal superintelligence to everyone,” with Muse as the vehicle an always available agent that can “understand their goals and can just work on their behalf 24/7.” Muse Wonder’s Active Memory, Active Focus, multi-agent delegation, and Secure VM architecture are the concrete tools to deliver that vision at consumer, small business, and enterprise scale. Falling behind would leave Meta’s massive distribution and product surface dependent on others’ models and infrastructure.

For Dr. @LisaSu , the same race is equally decisive for AMD. She has described demand as “very, very high for the next several years,” noting that even after capacity expansions “the demand is even higher than our supply,” and that the company will “substantially increase our supply in 2027.” On the specific impact of agents, Su has been explicit: agentic AI is “increasing the need for server CPU compute” for orchestration, data movement, and parallel execution, making CPU demand “largely additive” to GPU demand. She has observed the traditional CPU to GPU ratio shifting from 1:4 or 1:8 toward 1-4-8 CPU : 1 GPU, and potentially beyond, with “lots and lots of agents” driving more CPUs racks than GPUs. Meta’s Muse (@OpenAI  Dots, $MSFT, $AMZN, $GOOGL, @AnthropicAI , $AAPL   and similar smaller platforms) running persistent, multi-agent sandboxes on high density EPYC processors turns that thesis into volume. Winning the agentic layer with the right CPUs and rack scale systems (including designs like Helion) locks in years of data center growth; losing it cedes the fastest expanding part of the compute stack.

Moments in the History of Images: How Text-to-Image Models Changed Image-Making

Text-to-image models have transformed the way we create images. Today, systems like Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, FLUX, Adobe Firefly, Google Imagen, Nano Banana, Ideogram, Recraft, ByteDance Seedream, and OpenAI GPT Image can generate highly realistic images from just a few words. But in 2021, this technology was still in its infancy. One of the earliest examples of this idea was proposed by @elmanmansimov in his 2015 alignDRAW paper, and it took years for researchers to develop models capable of producing convincing images. The arrival of DALL·E in 2021 marked a turning point. Rather than spending days or weeks training a GAN model, artists could generate images almost instantly through text prompts. This shorter feedback loop opened up new possibilities for experimentation, allowing artists like @hollyherndon and @matdryhurst to improvise and collaborate with machines in ways that had previously been impossible.

During their early access to DALL·E 1, Herndon and Dryhurst created Infinite Images ∞, a series that explored the possibility of extending images beyond their original boundaries. The works reflect their belief that anyone should be able to create, adapt, and build upon the work of others. Produced in 2021–2022, these images were among the earliest artistic experiments with DALL·E 1, a research model available only to a small group of invited collaborators and OpenAI researchers. Today, DALL·E itself has been retired, but the technology it helped introduce has evolved into image-generation systems used by millions of people.

Working with DALL·E 1 and OpenAI's experimental InPaint system, the artists developed a technique for extending images piece by piece, maintaining continuity of style and subject matter across increasingly large compositions. Rather than relying solely on text prompts, they explored how images could grow through their relationships with one another. Although today's models can produce remarkably realistic results, these early experiments show how Herndon and Dryhurst were already pushing the technology beyond its intended uses, exploring its creative potential and capacity to engage with different artistic traditions. Infinite Images ∞ draws on a wide range of references, from surreal imaginary creatures to the bright colors of Fauvism and the grainy textures of gouache painting. For the artists, the possibility of infinite images extends across the entire history of human image-making, both past and future, increasingly shaped through collaboration between humans and machines.

How @AxisRobotics Is Helping Robots Learn From Experience

Teaching robots to work in the real world is not easy.

Unlike AI models that learn from huge amounts of text on the internet, robots need examples of how to move objects, complete tasks, and handle unexpected situations.

Axis Robotics is trying to solve this problem by allowing people to help train robots through a simple browser.

Here is how it works.

You control a simulated robot arm and teach it how to perform a task. If the robot makes a mistake, you can step in and correct it. These demonstrations and corrections become useful training data.

The robot can then learn from that data and try again.

This creates a continuous learning cycle:

People demonstrate tasks.
Robots learn from the examples.
Mistakes reveal what needs improvement.
New training focuses on those weaknesses.

Over time, this process can help robots become better at completing tasks.

Another important part is sim to real learning. A robot might perform perfectly in a virtual environment but struggle when handling real objects. Differences in weight, friction, and shape can change the outcome.

That is why collecting more data is not always enough. The data must also be useful and relevant to real world tasks.

Axis also introduced the $AXIS token, with allocations for ecosystem development and contributor rewards. The goal is to support the people who help improve the system.

The bigger idea is simple.

Axis Robotics wants to make robot training more accessible, allowing people to contribute without expensive equipment.

Instead of treating mistakes as wasted effort, the system uses them to identify what robots need to learn next.

The important question now is how effectively this training can help robots perform better in the physical world.

Better data could lead to better robots, and Axis is building a system designed to make that possible.
